rv.q: She is luminous, raw and full of grace, the embodiment of an extraordinary act of connection and communion that transcends theatre.
This is in every sense a work of art, as tough and weighty as it is fiercely beautiful.
Delivered with consummate composure by Rose, it has the force of ritual.

She’s enacting an attempt to smash the weighty legacy of the Atlantic slave trade. The gesture is cathartic — the block splinters dramatically — but the evidence of the past can never be annihilated. In part this is a travelogue, recounting Thompson’s efforts to retrace Britain’s slaving routes.

It's a heavy story made endurable by Rose's grounded performance, small breaths of humour, and by the strength of the writing itself; if Rose can – must – go through this journey of racism and imperialism, so can we.
This is a lovely piece of writing, expertly delivered and could well have many viewers in tears as well as raptures.
In Dawn Walton’s engrossing production, Rose is dressed in a symbolically white dress, and her performance is a warm mixture of passionate anger and intimate confessional.

cn.t: Critics largely acclaim *Salt* as a poetic, powerful meditation on the Atlantic slave trade, with Rochelle Rose's performance and the visceral sledgehammer imagery earning particular praise. A few find it uneven, but most call it vital, necessary theatre.
